:::caution[On main, next release]
This page was written from `main` at 9d25dc1. HotLoop 4.17.0 is the latest release, and it does not have what this page describes. An install from 4.17.0 will not match this page.
:::

Tell HotLoop where the plant is and it knows where the sun is. Sunrise, sunset,
dawn, dusk, solar noon, the sun's height and its bearing, all worked out on the
box from a latitude and a longitude. No weather service, no API key, no
internet. A site whose uplink died three weeks ago still turns the yard lights
on at dusk, which is the whole reason this isn't a call to somebody's cloud.

## Setting it up

Two variables, decimal degrees, north and east positive:

| Variable | Example | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `HOTLOOP_SITE_LATITUDE` | `41.4993` | north positive |
| `HOTLOOP_SITE_LONGITUDE` | `-81.6944` | east positive, so everywhere in the Americas is negative |

In the chart they're `plant.latitude` and `plant.longitude`. Both or neither.
Half a location, a number off the planet, or `41°29'58"N` stops HotLoop at
startup with the variable named, because a sunrise worked out from a typo
is hours wrong and looks perfectly reasonable on a screen. Get the numbers off
any map: right click, copy the coordinates.

Leave them out and there are no sun entities, and a rule with a sun trigger
isn't armed (the system log says which two variables to set). The Settings
screen shows both, read-only. A sunrise is something rules fire on, so it moves
with a reviewed deploy.

## The entities

| Entity | State | <span class="sr-only">Details</span> |
|---|---|---|
| `binary_sensor.sun_up` | `on` from sunrise to sunset | attributes `next_dawn`, `next_sunrise`, `next_noon`, `next_sunset`, `next_dusk`, in the site's timezone |
| `sensor.sun_elevation` | degrees above the horizon, negative below | whole degrees |
| `sensor.sun_azimuth` | degrees clockwise from true north, 90 is east | whole degrees |

They're platform `sun`, they read, and they take no services. `sun_up` is
worked out exactly, so it flips on the same second the sunrise and sunset
triggers fire, not off the rounded elevation.

Elevation and azimuth are whole degrees on purpose. The sun moves about a
quarter of a degree a minute. At a tenth of a degree that's a new state, a
logbook row and a history point every 24 seconds, all day, every day, per
sensor, for precision nobody automates on. A rule that wants "the sun is more
than 10 degrees up" gets it to the degree.

Under the midnight sun or in the polar night, the next sunset or sunrise can be
weeks away, and the attribute says when. If there isn't one within a year it
says `none within a year` instead of being quietly left out.

## Triggers

```json
{"type": "sun", "event": "sunset", "offsetSec": -1800}
```

`dawn`, `sunrise`, `noon`, `sunset` or `dusk`, moved by `offsetSec` (negative is
before, at most six hours either way). See
[AUTOMATIONS.md](/iot/automations/#sun-triggers). `binary_sensor.sun_up` works with
an ordinary `state` trigger too, and with `states['binary_sensor.sun_up'] ==
'off'` in a condition, for "only after dark".

## What the numbers mean

- **Sunrise and sunset** are when the top edge of the sun is on the horizon,
  with the standard allowance for the air bending the light: the center 0.833
  degrees below the horizon. That's what every almanac and every phone means
  by sunrise.
- **Dawn and dusk** are civil twilight, the center 6 degrees below. It's the
  line outdoor lighting is written around: after civil dusk you need lights to
  work outside.
- **Solar noon** is when the sun is due south (due north, south of the
  equator) and highest. It's rarely 12:00 on the clock; on the western edge of
  a timezone in summer it's well after one.
- **Elevation** is where the sun looks, corrected for refraction. Azimuth is
  from true north, not magnetic.

The flat-horizon caveat: these are for a sea-level horizon. A plant in a
valley loses the sun behind the ridge before sunset, and HotLoop doesn't know
about the ridge. Put an offset on the trigger.

## How we know it's right

The math is NOAA's: the equations behind the Global Monitoring Laboratory's
solar calculator (gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc), which are Jean Meeus's
*Astronomical Algorithms*. Ported as they are, the odd bit included (NOAA's
solar noon reads the equation of time around midnight UT rather than at noon,
worth seconds, and kept so we match NOAA to the second).

`internal/sun/testdata` holds the sunrise, sunset and solar noon tables NOAA's
calculator published for 2026 at six places, every cell copied as printed:
Cleveland and Austin (both sides of a daylight saving change), London (on the
meridian), Sydney (southern hemisphere), Quito (on the equator) and Utqiagvik,
north of the Arctic Circle, with two months of polar night and nearly three of
midnight sun. The test reads all 4,380 sunrise and sunset cells and holds every
crossing to the minute NOAA printed, plus two seconds, and every one of the
2,190 noons to within a second.
About 97 percent round to exactly the same minute; the rest are a second or so
from a half minute, which is two calculators disagreeing in the last digit,
not about the sun. Every day NOAA says has no sunrise or no sunset, HotLoop
says the same.

NOAA publishes no twilight table, so dawn and dusk are held to their
definition instead: at the moment HotLoop says it's dusk, the same position
math puts the sun's center 6 degrees down, to a fiftieth of a degree.

NOAA says its method is good to about a minute between the polar circles and
gets worse toward the poles, where the sun skims the horizon and a tiny error
in its height is minutes on the clock. Utqiagvik passes the same bar as
everywhere else. At the poles themselves the day-by-day method can miss the
one sunrise of the year; if you're running a plant at the South Pole, put a
schedule on it.
